notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::01 STACKIT Foundations
notes.front: What is STACKIT, and what is its core positioning as a cloud provider?
notes.back:
• European sovereign cloud platform of the Schwarz Group (Lidl, Kaufland), launched commercially 2019/2020.
  • Data centers exclusively in Germany and Austria; primary region eu01 with availability zones eu01-1/2/3.
  • Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) layer is built on OpenStack.
  • Positioning: digital sovereignty — EU data residency, General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) compliance, no exposure to the US CLOUD Act; certifications such as ISO 27001 and BSI C5.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::01 STACKIT Foundations
notes.front: Describe the STACKIT resource hierarchy and what a Project represents.
notes.back:
• Hierarchy: Organization → Folder(s) → Project.
  • A Project is the unit of resource ownership, Identity and Access Management (IAM) role assignment, quotas, and billing attribution — comparable to a Google Cloud Platform (GCP) project or an Azure resource group + subscription hybrid.
  • Folders group projects (e.g., per business unit or environment) and allow role inheritance downward.
  • Landing-zone practice: project per team × environment (e.g., payments-dev, payments-prod).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::01 STACKIT Foundations
notes.front: Which identity types exist in STACKIT Identity and Access Management (IAM), and how do machines authenticate?
notes.back:
• User accounts (portal login) and service accounts (machine identities, scoped to a project).
  • Members get roles (e.g., owner, editor, reader, plus service-specific roles) on organization, folder, or project.
  • Service accounts authenticate via:
    • Key flow — RSA key pair, client signs a JSON Web Token (JWT) and exchanges it for a short-lived access token (preferred for Terraform).
    • Token flow — static long-lived token (simpler, weaker; rotate!).
    • OpenID Connect (OIDC) federation — exchange a Continuous Integration (CI) workload token for STACKIT credentials, i.e. keyless pipelines.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::01 STACKIT Foundations
notes.front: Which four interfaces can you use to manage STACKIT resources programmatically or interactively?
notes.back:
1. STACKIT Portal (web UI, self-service).
  2. STACKIT CLI (stackit) — also acts as a kubectl credential helper.
  3. REST APIs + SDKs (Go, Python, Java, JavaScript).
  4. Terraform provider stackitcloud/stackit — the standard for Infrastructure as Code (IaC).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::01 STACKIT Foundations
notes.front: Name the main STACKIT runtime/compute offerings and their rough analogues.
notes.back:
• Compute Engine — OpenStack virtual machines (flavors incl. general purpose g1.x, memory/compute optimized, GPU). ≈ EC2.
  • STACKIT Kubernetes Engine (SKE) — managed Kubernetes. ≈ GKE/AKS/EKS.
  • Cloud Foundry — Platform as a Service (PaaS) for pushing apps without cluster management.
  • Confidential Server / Confidential Kubernetes — in-memory-encrypted compute for highly sensitive workloads (limited availability).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::01 STACKIT Foundations
notes.front: List the managed data services STACKIT offers.
notes.back:
• PostgreSQL Flex, MongoDB Flex, SQL Server Flex, MariaDB — relational/NoSQL databases with high-availability plans and automated backups.
  • Redis — in-memory cache/store.
  • OpenSearch — search and log analytics.
  • RabbitMQ and PubSub — messaging.
  • Architectural note: prefer these over self-operating stateful workloads inside SKE unless you need features/versions they lack — state is the hard part of multi-cluster.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::01 STACKIT Foundations
notes.front: Which storage classes of service exist on STACKIT, and which Kubernetes access modes do they map to?
notes.back:
• Block Storage (OpenStack Cinder; multiple performance classes, e.g. storage_premium_perfX) → PersistentVolumes, ReadWriteOnce (RWO).
  • File storage / NFS Shares → ReadWriteMany (RWX) volumes.
  • Object Storage — S3-compatible; buckets + credential groups. Used for backups (Velero), Terraform state, Loki chunks, registry backends.
  • Backup Storage — cost-optimized, geo-redundant target for volume backups.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::01 STACKIT Foundations
notes.front: Which STACKIT services cover security & developer tooling (secrets, keys, images, code)?
notes.back:
• Secrets Manager — managed storage/rotation of secrets, portal-integrated.
  • Key Management Service (KMS) — cryptographic key operations, envelope encryption.
  • Container Registry — private Open Container Initiative (OCI) registry with access control and vulnerability scanning.
  • STACKIT Git — managed Git repositories.
  • Run Command — remote script execution on Compute Engine instances without direct SSH.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::01 STACKIT Foundations
notes.front: Which STACKIT services cover observability, and what stack are they based on?
notes.back:
• STACKIT Observability (formerly Argus — that name is deprecated): managed Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Tempo for metrics, logs, traces, alerting.
  • Logs / LogMe — centralized log ingestion, storage, and search.
  • Telemetry Router — centralized handling of audit streams.
  • SKE clusters can be wired to an Observability instance via a cluster extension.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::01 STACKIT Foundations
notes.front: Name the STACKIT networking products relevant to a hybrid platform design.
notes.back:
• STACKIT Network Area (SNA) — organization-level network layer connecting projects privately; hub for hybrid connectivity.
  • VPN — managed IPsec site-to-site service into the SNA.
  • Network Load Balancer (Layer 4) and Application Load Balancer (Layer 7, host/path routing, Web Application Firewall (WAF) option).
  • DNS — hosted zones/record sets (works with external-dns).
  • Security Groups (stateful instance firewalls) and Unified Firewall (beta; central rule management across projects).
  • Content Delivery Network (CDN).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::01 STACKIT Foundations
notes.front: Why is STACKIT specifically attractive for workloads under Dutch/EU public-sector compliance regimes (BIO2, NIS2), and what do YOU still have to do?
notes.back:
• Provider side: EU-only data residency (DE/AT), GDPR alignment, no US CLOUD Act exposure, ISO 27001 / BSI C5 attestations — strong answers for sovereignty questions in Baseline Informatiebeveiliging Overheid 2 (BIO2) and Network and Information Security 2 (NIS2) assessments.
  • Your side (shared responsibility): environment zoning/segmentation, access control and joiner-mover-leaver via your Active Directory (AD), central audit logging, encryption configuration, incident response, and demonstrable control of the deployment chain (GitOps + signed images help).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: What is the STACKIT Kubernetes Engine (SKE), and which open-source project is it built on?
notes.back:
• SKE is STACKIT's managed, Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF)-conformant Kubernetes service.
  • Built on Gardener (open-sourced by SAP): a Kubernetes-native system that manages fleets of clusters using Kubernetes itself.
  • STACKIT operates the control planes; you get self-service cluster creation via Portal, CLI, API, or Terraform, with auto-updates and automatic repair.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: Explain Gardener's Garden / Seed / Shoot model and where your SKE cluster fits in.
notes.back:
• Garden cluster — the central management cluster running Gardener itself.
  • Seed clusters — provider-operated clusters that host the control planes (kube-apiserver, etcd, controllers) of customer clusters as pods.
  • Shoot cluster — your cluster: its control plane lives in a STACKIT-managed seed; only the worker nodes run as Compute Engine VMs inside your project.
  • Consequence: you never see or SSH the control plane; control-plane scaling, high availability (HA), and etcd backups are STACKIT's job.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: Which properties do you configure per SKE node pool?
notes.back:
• Machine type/flavor (e.g., g1.3), and min/max node count for autoscaling.
  • Availability zones (eu01-1/2/3) — spread pools across zones for HA.
  • Boot volume size and type (block-storage performance class).
  • Node operating system: Flatcar Container Linux (immutable, auto-updating).
  • Kubernetes labels and taints — the basis for tenant/workload placement.
  • Multiple pools per cluster are normal: e.g., system pool, tenant pools, GPU pool.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: How does SKE handle Kubernetes version and node OS updates, and what must an architect plan around?
notes.back:
• Auto-updates for Kubernetes patch versions and Flatcar OS run inside a configurable maintenance window.
  • Each Kubernetes minor version has a support window; expired versions get force-upgraded — you cannot pin forever.
  • Plan: stagger maintenance windows across the fleet (canary ring first), keep PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs) correct so node drains don't take services down, and test against version skew (kubectl/API deprecations) continuously.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: What is SKE cluster hibernation and when is it useful?
notes.back:
• Scheduled temporary shutdown of a cluster (control plane and worker nodes are stopped/scaled to zero).
  • Cuts cost for non-production clusters, e.g., dev/test clusters hibernating nights and weekends.
  • Trade-off: wake-up latency; unsuitable for anything that must receive traffic or run background jobs. In a many-cluster tenancy model, hibernation makes cluster-per-team affordable for dev.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: Which autoscaling mechanisms are available on SKE, and at which layers?
notes.back:
• Node layer: Cluster Autoscaler per node pool between configured min/max.
  • Pod layer: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) and Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA).
  • Event-driven: Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling (KEDA) — scale on queue depth, etc.; SKE advertises event-driven autoscaling support.
  • Architectural note: autoscaler limits are also a tenancy quota — a runaway tenant can only grow to the pool max.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: Which three ways exist to obtain credentials for an SKE cluster, and what are the security trade-offs?
notes.back:
1. Admin kubeconfig — client-certificate based, expiry up to 180 days. Coarse revocation: rotating credentials invalidates all admin kubeconfigs and ServiceAccount tokens. Treat as break-glass, store offline.
  2. CLI login — stackit ske kubeconfig login as a kubectl exec plugin; fetches short-lived credentials on demand via your STACKIT identity. Good default for operators.
  3. STACKIT Identity Provider (IDP) integration — enable per cluster, then bind Kubernetes Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) RoleBindings to user email addresses; users log in with STACKIT accounts.
None of these speak your corporate Active Directory (AD) directly — that gap drives the PingFederate/Pinniped designs in the Identity subdeck.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: What happens when you create a Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer on SKE (2026 state)?
notes.back:
• The cloud controller manager provisions a STACKIT Load Balancer (Layer 4, TCP/UDP) with a public IP; the LB resources appear (and are billed) in your project.
  • History: clusters created before June 2024 used yawol (STACKIT's open-source OpenStack LB operator, LB = small VMs in your project); new clusters use the dedicated Load Balancer service.
  • HTTP(S)/Layer 7: run your own ingress controller behind the L4 LB, or use the Application Load Balancer SKE extension (was in preview).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: Which Service annotations/fields matter for SKE load balancers in a hybrid design?
notes.back:
• Internal LB annotation — LB gets a private IP in the node network instead of a public IP → the way to expose services only to on-prem over the VPN.
  • spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges — Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) allow-list of callers (add on-prem ranges; include pod CIDR if pods must reach it).
  • PROXY protocol v2 annotation (lb.stackit.cloud/...) — preserves client source IPs to the backend.
  • Session persistence with source IP is available via annotation.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: How is persistent storage provided in SKE, and where do its limits push you architecturally?
notes.back:
• Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver on OpenStack Cinder block storage; StorageClasses map to performance tiers; ReadWriteOnce (RWO) only; volumes are zone-bound → StatefulSets must respect zones.
  • ReadWriteMany (RWX) via NFS/file-storage offerings.
  • Volume snapshots via CSI → enables Velero backups to Object Storage.
  • Push: for multi-cluster or Disaster Recovery (DR), prefer managed databases and Object Storage over cluster-local volumes — block storage does not replicate across clusters.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: Describe the default network posture of SKE worker nodes and the API server, and how to harden API access.
notes.back:
• Nodes are private — no public IPs (and you can't mark them public at creation). Inbound only via load balancers; outbound via provider NAT.
  • The kube-apiserver endpoint is public by default (it lives in the STACKIT seed, not your network).
  • Hardening: enable the Access Control List (ACL) extension to allow-list CIDRs (e.g., only your on-prem egress IPs / VPN ranges); private API-server access patterns exist for reaching it from within the STACKIT network — verify current options per cluster.
  • Cluster metadata such as the pod CIDR is exposed in the shoot-info ConfigMap (kube-system).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: Which official SKE cluster extensions can you toggle (e.g., via Terraform), and what do they do?
notes.back:
• observability — wires the cluster to a STACKIT Observability instance (the old argus block is deprecated).
  • dns — cluster DNS domain integration with STACKIT DNS.
  • acl — API-server access allow-listing.
  • application_load_balancer — managed Layer 7 ingress (private preview initially).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: How do you provision an SKE cluster and then Kubernetes resources in one Terraform run, and what is the main pitfall?
notes.back:
• stackit_ske_cluster creates the cluster; stackit_ske_kubeconfig (with refresh = true) yields credentials; feed host/CA/client certs into the kubernetes/helm providers.
  • Alternative: exec-plugin auth in the provider using stackit ske kubeconfig login → no long-lived certs in state.
  • Pitfalls: kubeconfig material lands in Terraform state (encrypt/protect the backend!); provider-inside-same-apply ordering is fragile — better: Terraform bootstraps only the GitOps agent, everything else via GitOps.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: An SKE cluster is 'managed' — which platform components do YOU still own (the day-2 stack)?
notes.back:
• Ingress controller + certificates (cert-manager), external-dns.
  • GitOps agent (Argo CD/Flux), policy engine (Kyverno/Gatekeeper).
  • Secrets sync (External Secrets Operator), workload identity story.
  • Observability agents (Grafana Alloy / OpenTelemetry (OTel) collector), Velero backups.
  • Registry credentials, image policy/signing, NetworkPolicies, ResourceQuotas.
  • This 'golden stack' must be identical across the fleet — that is the real multi-cluster problem, and why it lives in Git, not in hand-applied manifests.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: What determines SKE's cost model, and which two levers reduce non-production spend?
notes.back:
• You pay a fee for the managed control plane per cluster plus normal Compute Engine/storage/LB prices for workers.
  • Lever 1: hibernation schedules for dev/test clusters.
  • Lever 2: autoscaling node pools with low minimums (scale-to-few), right-sized flavors.
  • Tenancy consequence: per-cluster fees make 'a cluster for everyone' more expensive than namespaces — quantify this in the multitenancy decision.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::02 SKE Core
notes.front: How does NetworkPolicy behave on SKE and why must a platform team set defaults?
notes.back:
• SKE ships a Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin that enforces the standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy API — but Kubernetes' default is allow-all between pods across all namespaces.
  • Platform baseline: default-deny ingress (and ideally egress) per tenant namespace, then explicit allows; permit kube-dns; document how tenants request cross-namespace flows.
  • Note: you don't control which CNI or its low-level config on a managed cluster — don't design around CNI-specific features you can't guarantee fleet-wide.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::03 IaaS & Networking
notes.front: What are the building blocks of STACKIT Compute Engine?
notes.back:
• OpenStack-based virtual machines: flavors (general purpose g1.x, compute-/memory-optimized, GPU incl. NVIDIA A100), placed in an availability zone.
  • Boot volume (from an image — Ubuntu, Flatcar, Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), Windows...) + attachable data volumes (block storage).
  • Attached to project networks; firewalled by security groups; optionally a public IP.
  • Relevant even in a Kubernetes-centric design: VPN test endpoints, jump hosts, self-managed appliances.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::03 IaaS & Networking
notes.front: How is STACKIT Block Storage tiered, and what operational features does it have?
notes.back:
• Multiple performance classes (e.g., storage_premium_perfX with increasing input/output operations per second (IOPS) per class) — chosen per volume / per StorageClass in SKE.
  • Volumes are zonal; snapshots and backups supported (Backup Storage as geo-redundant target).
  • Based on OpenStack Cinder → this is what the SKE Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver provisions.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::03 IaaS & Networking
notes.front: What is STACKIT Object Storage and what six roles does it typically play in a platform architecture?
notes.back:
• S3-compatible object store; access via credential groups + access/secret keys per bucket scope.
  • Typical platform roles:
    1. Velero backup target
    2. Terraform state backend (see locking caveat card)
    3. Loki/Tempo/Thanos chunk storage
    4. Registry storage backend
    5. Artifact/report storage for CI
    6. Data exchange with on-prem without opening databases
  • Keep backup traffic cloud-local — do not haul it over the VPN.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::03 IaaS & Networking
notes.front: What is a STACKIT Network Area (SNA) and why is it the cornerstone of a multi-project + hybrid design?
notes.back:
• An organization-level networking construct: a centrally administered pool of IP ranges from which member projects get their networks.
  • Connects multiple projects privately (no public internet transit) — the STACKIT answer to a shared Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) / hub-and-spoke.
  • Hybrid: VPN and Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) connections terminate into the SNA, making on-prem routes available to all attached projects.
  • Central Internet Protocol Address Management (IPAM) + route governance by the platform team; project teams consume.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::03 IaaS & Networking
notes.front: Trade-off: one shared SNA for the whole organization vs. isolated per-project networking. When do you choose which?
notes.back:
Shared SNAIsolated projects
ConnectivityPrivate project↔project and single hybrid hubEach project needs its own path (or public endpoints)
GovernanceCentral IPAM, non-overlapping CIDRs enforcedNone needed; CIDRs may overlap
Blast radiusMisrouting/compromise can propagate; needs security groups + firewall disciplineHard network isolation by default
FitPlatform-managed landing zone, hybrid mandatory (your case)Fully independent tenants, no shared services
Hybrid + central management effectively forces the SNA; compensate with segmentation (security groups, Unified Firewall, NetworkPolicy).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::03 IaaS & Networking
notes.front: How do STACKIT security groups behave, and what is the Unified Firewall?
notes.back:
• Security groups: stateful firewall rule sets attached to instances/interfaces; default posture blocks inbound until allowed; reusable across servers.
  • Unified Firewall (beta): central dashboard combining security groups, database Access Control Lists (ACLs), and public-IP rules across projects, with rule templates — the tool for a platform team enforcing one policy over many projects.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::03 IaaS & Networking
notes.front: Describe the managed STACKIT VPN service: protocol, topology, routing, HA, and throughput.
notes.back:
• Managed IPsec (IKEv2) gateways attached to a STACKIT Network Area (SNA).
  • Topology: site-to-site and site-to-multisite. No point-to-site/client VPN.
  • Routing: policy-based, static, or dynamic via Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) (BGP recommended for HA failover).
  • High availability: gateways are active-active pairs with parallel tunnels.
  • Service plans from 100 Mbit/s to 1,000 Mbit/s (plan upgrade possible with brief interruption).
  • No NAT support → on-prem and SNA address space must not overlap.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::03 IaaS & Networking
notes.front: Trade-off: managed STACKIT VPN vs. self-managed VPN VMs (strongSwan/WireGuard) vs. MPLS/dedicated line for on-prem connectivity.
notes.back:
• Managed VPN: + no ops, HA built-in, BGP; − ≤1 Gbit/s, IPsec only, no NAT, no client VPN, internet-dependent latency/jitter.
  • Self-managed on Compute Engine: + full control (WireGuard, NAT, policy quirks, client VPN possible); − you own HA, patching, monitoring; still internet transport.
  • MPLS / dedicated connectivity into the SNA: + predictable latency/bandwidth, private transport (compliance-friendly); − cost, lead time, carrier contracts.
  • Common pattern: start managed VPN; add MPLS when bandwidth/latency/compliance demands it; keep VPN as backup path (BGP handles failover).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::03 IaaS & Networking
notes.front: Compare STACKIT Network Load Balancer and Application Load Balancer — and when do you use neither and run your own ingress?
notes.back:
• Network Load Balancer (NLB): Layer 4, TCP/UDP, PROXY protocol for client IPs; what SKE Services of type LoadBalancer create.
  • Application Load Balancer (ALB): Layer 7 HTTP(S), host/path/header routing, TLS termination, Web Application Firewall (WAF) option.
  • Own ingress controller (ingress-nginx, Envoy Gateway, Traefik) behind an NLB: maximal feature control (canary, auth hooks, custom middlewares), identical config across clusters and on-prem — usually the right call for a hybrid fleet; managed ALB reduces ops for simpler setups.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::03 IaaS & Networking
notes.front: How does the STACKIT DNS service fit into a Kubernetes platform, and what tooling automates it?
notes.back:
• Hosted zones + record sets with API/Terraform support.
  • Automate records from Kubernetes with external-dns (webhook based provider support) pointing at cluster ingress/LB IPs.
  • In hybrid: STACKIT DNS holds the cloud/public zones; corporate zones stay on the on-prem Active Directory (AD) DNS — see the split-horizon card in the Hybrid subdeck.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::03 IaaS & Networking
notes.front: Trade-off: managed database (e.g., PostgreSQL Flex) vs. running a Kubernetes operator (e.g., CloudNativePG) inside SKE.
notes.back:
• Managed (PostgreSQL Flex): + HA plans, automated backups/patching, survives cluster rebuilds, offloads ops; − version/extension lag, less tuning control, per-instance cost, network hop from pods.
  • In-cluster operator: + latest versions/extensions, cluster-local latency, GitOps-native config, fine-grained multi-tenant packing; − you own backup/restore correctness, upgrades, failover testing; DB dies with the cluster unless backups/DR are solid.
  • Heuristic: production system-of-record → managed; ephemeral/dev, per-tenant micro-DBs, or special extensions → operator.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::03 IaaS & Networking
notes.front: Which quota layers exist on STACKIT/SKE and how do they compose into tenant limits?
notes.back:
1. Project quotas — caps on cores, RAM, volumes, public IPs per project (raiseable via support).
  2. Node pool min/max — hard ceiling on cluster compute.
  3. Kubernetes ResourceQuota — per-namespace CPU/memory/object caps.
  4. LimitRange — per-pod/container defaults and bounds (forces requests to be set, protecting the scheduler).
Tenancy design = deciding at which of these layers a 'tenant' is throttled.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::04 Identity, Access & Secrets
notes.front: Enumerate the four identity planes in a hybrid STACKIT platform and what asserts identity in each.
notes.back:
1. Cloud control plane — STACKIT Identity and Access Management (IAM): users + service accounts, roles on org/folder/project.
  2. Kubernetes API plane — kubeconfigs, OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens, Kubernetes Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).
  3. Application plane — end-user single sign-on (SSO) via PingFederate (OIDC/SAML) in front of workloads.
  4. Machine plane — STACKIT service accounts, Kubernetes ServiceAccounts, CI workload identities, registry robot accounts.
Architect's job: one source of truth (Active Directory (AD)) projected into all four, with joiner-mover-leaver working end to end.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::04 Identity, Access & Secrets
notes.front: Why can Kubernetes not authenticate users against LDAP/Active Directory directly, and what is the standard bridge?
notes.back:
• kube-apiserver has no Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) authenticator. Supported user authN: client certificates, static/bootstrap tokens, OpenID Connect (OIDC), or webhook token authentication.
  • Standard bridge: an OIDC Provider (OP) federating to AD/LDAP — exactly what PingFederate does. It authenticates the user against AD and issues a JSON Web Token (JWT) ID token containing username + group claims.
  • Kubernetes validates the JWT signature against the issuer's published keys (JSON Web Key Set (JWKS)) — no per-request call to AD.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::04 Identity, Access & Secrets
notes.front: How do OIDC claims map to Kubernetes RBAC, and what is the recommended group-based design?
notes.back:
• API server maps the token's username claim (e.g., email) and groups claim to a Kubernetes user + group set, usually with a prefix (e.g., oidc:) to avoid collisions with built-ins.
  • Design: define persona ClusterRoles (platform-admin, tenant-admin, developer, viewer), then bind them to AD groups via (Cluster)RoleBindings with kind: Group.
  • Result: access management happens in AD group membership — no per-user changes in clusters; RoleBindings themselves are GitOps-managed and identical fleet-wide.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::04 Identity, Access & Secrets
notes.front: On a managed cluster like SKE you may not control kube-apiserver flags. Which architectures still give you PingFederate-based login, fleet-wide?
notes.back:
1. Native OIDC config, if the managed offering exposes it (SKE ships its own STACKIT IDP integration; support for customer-supplied issuers must be verified per current SKE feature set).
  2. Pinniped — Supervisor (one instance, federates to PingFederate as upstream OIDC) + Concierge per cluster (exchanges Supervisor tokens for cluster credentials via TokenCredentialRequest). Works without touching apiserver flags; one login config for the whole fleet.
  3. kube-oidc-proxy / authenticating reverse proxy in front of each API server — impersonates users after verifying OIDC; adds a hop and a critical component you operate.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::04 Identity, Access & Secrets
notes.front: Trade-off: per-cluster OIDC configuration vs. Pinniped for a multi-cluster fleet.
notes.back:
• Per-cluster OIDC: + no extra moving parts, native kubectl flows (kubelogin); − N client registrations in PingFederate or shared client per cluster, config drift risk, only possible where the managed offering exposes OIDC settings.
  • Pinniped: + single upstream integration, uniform login UX (pinniped get kubeconfig) across SKE + on-prem clusters, short-lived cluster certs, works on any conformant cluster; − you operate Supervisor (an availability-critical SPOF for interactive login) and Concierge agents; break-glass path still needed.
  • Hybrid fleets with mixed cluster types usually justify Pinniped.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::04 Identity, Access & Secrets
notes.front: Where does Dex fit relative to PingFederate, and do you need it if you already run PingFederate?
notes.back:
• Dex is a lightweight OIDC broker with connectors (LDAP, SAML, GitHub...) — commonly used to give Kubernetes an OIDC front for an LDAP directory.
  • If PingFederate already fronts your Active Directory as a full-featured OIDC/SAML provider, Dex is redundant for that job — adding it just adds a hop and an ops burden.
  • Legitimate niche: as an app-local broker where a component only supports a narrow OIDC dialect, or to decouple lab environments from enterprise change processes.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::04 Identity, Access & Secrets
notes.front: Design a break-glass access procedure for SKE clusters when the identity chain (VPN → PingFederate → AD) is down.
notes.back:
• Keep a sealed admin kubeconfig (client-cert, ≤180-day expiry) per cluster in an offline/escrowed secret store with dual control; calendar its renewal.
  • Alternative path: STACKIT CLI login by a platform owner account (depends on STACKIT IAM, not on your AD).
  • After use: run SKE credential rotation — note it invalidates ALL admin kubeconfigs and ServiceAccount tokens for that cluster; plan the blast radius.
  • Audit: alert on any use of break-glass credentials.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::04 Identity, Access & Secrets
notes.front: How should Terraform and CI pipelines authenticate to STACKIT, from least to most preferred?
notes.back:
1. Static service-account token — simplest, long-lived bearer secret; avoid.
  2. Service-account key flow — RSA private key signs a JWT exchanged for short-lived tokens; key still needs safekeeping (Vault/CI secret).
  3. OIDC workload identity federation — the Terraform provider accepts an OIDC request token/URL, so a CI job (e.g., GitLab CI ID token) authenticates as a STACKIT service account with no stored key at all.
Scope service accounts per project + least-privilege roles; one god-account for the whole org is the classic anti-pattern.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::04 Identity, Access & Secrets
notes.front: Compare the secret-management options for a hybrid STACKIT platform: STACKIT Secrets Manager, self-hosted Vault/OpenBao on-prem, sealed-secrets/SOPS in Git.
notes.back:
• STACKIT Secrets Manager: managed, cloud-local (low latency for cloud workloads), portal/API integrated; another store outside your DC's control sphere.
  • Central Vault/OpenBao on-prem: single sovereign source of truth, rich auth (LDAP!), dynamic secrets, audit; but every cloud read crosses the VPN → availability coupling, and you operate it in HA.
  • Sealed-secrets / SOPS (Secrets OPerationS) in Git: GitOps-native, no runtime store; but rotation is a commit, no dynamic secrets, key custody per cluster (sealed-secrets) or per KMS (SOPS).
  • Common hybrid answer: central Vault as source of truth + External Secrets Operator caching into cluster Secrets (tolerates short link outages), SOPS only for bootstrap material.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::04 Identity, Access & Secrets
notes.front: What does the External Secrets Operator (ESO) do in a multi-cluster design, and which failure mode must you plan for?
notes.back:
• ESO runs in each cluster, reads from external stores (Vault, STACKIT Secrets Manager, ...) via (Cluster)SecretStore configs, and materializes native Kubernetes Secrets from ExternalSecret manifests — manifests live in Git, values never do.
  • Fleet pattern: identical ExternalSecrets everywhere; per-cluster identity to the store scopes what each cluster may read (blast-radius control).
  • Failure mode: store unreachable (VPN down) → existing Secrets persist, but rotation and new secrets stall; set sane refresh intervals and alert on sync failures.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::04 Identity, Access & Secrets
notes.front: Which credentials does the container image supply chain need across the fleet, and how are they distributed?
notes.back:
• Pull credentials per cluster/namespace for your registry (Harbor robot accounts / STACKIT Container Registry credentials) → distribute as imagePullSecrets via External Secrets Operator or your GitOps bootstrap; wire into ServiceAccounts.
  • Push credentials only in CI, short-lived where possible.
  • Image trust: sign in CI (cosign), verify in-cluster with a policy engine (Kyverno verifyImages) — the enforcement manifest is part of the golden stack.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::04 Identity, Access & Secrets
notes.front: What is the role of a Key Management Service (KMS) in this architecture, and what stays outside your control on SKE?
notes.back:
• KMS (STACKIT KMS or on-prem Hardware Security Module (HSM)-backed) provides envelope encryption for application-level data, SOPS, and backup encryption — with key sovereignty as the compliance argument.
  • On SKE the control plane (including etcd and its encryption at rest) is operated by STACKIT — you configure workload-level crypto, not apiserver encryption providers.
  • Rule: anything you back up off-platform (Velero, DB dumps) is encrypted with keys YOU control.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::05 Multitenancy
notes.front: Define soft vs. hard multitenancy, and what question decides which one you need.
notes.back:
• Soft: tenants are trusted-but-separated (internal teams); isolation guards against accidents and noisy neighbors, not determined attackers.
  • Hard: tenants are mutually untrusted (external customers, differing security classifications); isolation must hold against deliberate escape attempts.
  • Deciding question: "What is the worst credible actor inside a tenant, and what may they never reach?" Compliance zoning (e.g., BIO2 classification levels, production vs. rest) often forces hard boundaries regardless of trust.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::05 Multitenancy
notes.front: Namespace-per-tenant on a shared SKE cluster: which SIX mechanisms combine to make it work?
notes.back:
1. RBAC — tenant admins scoped to their namespace(s).
  2. ResourceQuota — CPU/memory/object caps per namespace.
  3. LimitRange — per-pod defaults/bounds so quotas are enforceable.
  4. NetworkPolicy — default-deny between tenant namespaces.
  5. Admission policy (Kyverno/Gatekeeper) — forbid privileged pods, hostPath, node ports; enforce Pod Security Standards.
  6. PriorityClass / node placement — protect system workloads; optionally dedicated node pools per tenant via taints.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::05 Multitenancy
notes.front: What does namespace isolation NOT isolate? (The case against soft multitenancy)
notes.back:
• Control plane: one kube-apiserver + etcd — a tenant's request flood or huge object churn degrades everyone.
  • Cluster-scoped resources: CustomResourceDefinitions (CRDs), their versions, admission webhooks, ClusterRoles — tenants needing different operator versions collide.
  • Nodes/kernel: containers share kernels; a container escape lands on a node possibly running other tenants' pods.
  • Upgrades: one Kubernetes version and one maintenance window for all tenants.
  • DNS/service visibility unless additionally restricted.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::05 Multitenancy
notes.front: Cluster-per-tenant on SKE: pros and cons.
notes.back:
• Pros: real control-plane + node isolation, independent Kubernetes versions and CRDs, per-tenant blast radius, clean cost attribution (whole cluster), tenant-specific maintenance windows, simple offboarding (delete cluster).
  • Cons: per-cluster control-plane fee + baseline node cost (poor bin-packing), fleet sprawl → you MUST have fleet automation (Terraform + GitOps + ApplicationSets), slower global changes, N× observability/agents overhead.
  • SKE-specific mitigations: hibernation for dev tenants; small autoscaling pools.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::05 Multitenancy
notes.front: What is vCluster, and where does it sit between namespaces and full clusters?
notes.back:
• A virtual cluster: a real kube-apiserver + datastore running as pods inside a namespace of a host cluster; a syncer maps its pods onto host nodes.
  • Gives tenants: own API server (no CRD/webhook collisions, own versions, cluster-admin feeling), fast creation, cheap (no cloud control-plane fee).
  • Does NOT give: node/kernel isolation (workloads share host nodes), network isolation beyond host NetworkPolicy, independence from host outages.
  • Sweet spot: many dev/test tenants, platform-engineering self-service, CI ephemeral clusters — on top of a few well-governed SKE host clusters.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::05 Multitenancy
notes.front: Which tools implement 'namespace-as-a-service' style tenancy, and what do they add over raw namespaces?
notes.back:
• Capsule — Tenant CRD grouping multiple namespaces; tenant owners self-create namespaces within quota/policy guardrails.
  • Hierarchical Namespace Controller (HNC) — parent/child namespaces with policy propagation.
  • Kiosk / project-style operators — similar self-service abstractions.
  • Value: turns tenancy from a ticket-driven process into self-service with centrally enforced defaults (quotas, NetworkPolicies, RBAC templates propagated automatically).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::05 Multitenancy
notes.front: How do you achieve node-level isolation for a sensitive tenant inside a shared SKE cluster, and where is the ceiling?
notes.back:
• Dedicated node pool with taints; tenant workloads get tolerations + nodeSelector/affinity; admission policy prevents others from tolerating.
  • Result: no kernel/node sharing with other tenants — closes the container-escape-to-shared-node hole.
  • Ceiling: still shared control plane, CRDs, upgrades. Kernel-sandboxed runtimes (gVisor/Kata) are generally not configurable on managed SKE nodes — if you need them, that's a separate-cluster (or Confidential Kubernetes) decision.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::05 Multitenancy
notes.front: At the STACKIT layer: tenant = project vs. tenants sharing one project — trade-offs?
notes.back:
• Project per tenant/team-env: hard IAM boundary, own quotas, clean billing, independent service instances; SNA still gives private connectivity where wanted. Cost: more projects to govern → automate with Terraform landing-zone modules.
  • Shared project: less overhead, easy resource sharing; but IAM roles are project-wide (tenant separation collapses at cloud level), quota contention, murky cost attribution.
  • Guideline: cloud-level tenancy boundaries should be at least as strong as your strongest in-cluster boundary — don't run hard-isolated clusters of two tenants in one shared project with shared IAM.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::05 Multitenancy
notes.front: Give a decision matrix: which tenancy model for which situation (namespaces / vCluster / dedicated node pools / cluster-per-tenant)?
notes.back:
• Same org, trusted teams, standard workloads → namespaces + quotas + NetworkPolicy (cheapest, densest).
  • Teams needing own CRDs/operators/versions or cluster-admin → vCluster on shared hosts.
  • One tenant with elevated data sensitivity, rest standard → shared cluster + dedicated tainted node pool (+ stricter policies).
  • Untrusted tenants, prod/compliance zones, regulatory separation → cluster-per-tenant (per zone), separate projects.
  • Drivers to weigh: trust level, compliance zoning, cost per tenant, ops maturity, upgrade independence, blast radius.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::05 Multitenancy
notes.front: How is network multitenancy enforced inside a shared cluster, and what is the correct default?
notes.back:
• Correct default: default-deny ingress AND egress NetworkPolicy per tenant namespace, shipped automatically with namespace creation (Capsule/GitOps template).
  • Explicit allows: kube-dns, ingress-controller → tenant services, tenant-internal traffic, named cross-tenant flows.
  • Egress governance: restrict which tenants may reach on-prem ranges over the VPN — the hybrid link is itself a shared, capacity-limited resource.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::05 Multitenancy
notes.front: How do you multitenant the shared platform services — ingress and monitoring — and what are the trade-offs?
notes.back:
• Ingress: one shared controller (+ IngressClass, per-tenant hostname policy, rate limits) = cheap, single LB; per-tenant controllers = config blast-radius isolation and independent tuning at N× LB cost.
  • Monitoring: shared Prometheus with tenant labels + query federation = cheap but cardinality abuse by one tenant hurts all; per-tenant agents shipping to a multi-tenant backend (Mimir/Thanos or STACKIT Observability instances per tenant) scales cleaner.
  • Watch: quotas exist for compute, but rarely for metric cardinality, log volume, ingress config size — set explicit limits there too.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::05 Multitenancy
notes.front: How does Argo CD support multitenancy so tenants can self-serve deployments safely?
notes.back:
• AppProjects constrain: allowed source repos, destination clusters/namespaces, permitted resource kinds (e.g., forbid ClusterRole), and orphaned-resource monitoring.
  • Tenant RBAC in Argo CD (SSO groups from PingFederate!) maps AD groups → AppProject roles.
  • Pattern: platform team owns the golden-stack Applications; each tenant gets an AppProject + ApplicationSet generating their apps per cluster — self-service within guardrails.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::06 Multi-Cluster & GitOps
notes.front: List the legitimate reasons to run MULTIPLE clusters instead of one big one.
notes.back:
• Environment separation (dev/test/prod) with independent upgrade cadence.
  • Tenant/compliance isolation (hard boundaries, BIO2/NIS2 zones).
  • Blast-radius control — a bad rollout, poisoned CRD, or control-plane outage stays local.
  • Upgrade canarying — rings of clusters take new Kubernetes/platform versions first.
  • Placement — on-prem + STACKIT (hybrid), later multi-provider.
  • Scale/limits — avoid mega-cluster etcd and upgrade risk.
  • Anti-reason: 'one cluster per microservice' — cluster count must stay proportional to your automation maturity.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::06 Multi-Cluster & GitOps
notes.front: Describe the management-cluster (hub) + workload-clusters pattern as used on STACKIT.
notes.back:
• A small, hardened admin/management cluster runs the fleet machinery: Argo CD (or Flux controllers), External Secrets tooling, backup orchestration, observability aggregation, possibly Terraform runners.
  • Workload clusters stay boring: golden stack + tenant apps, everything reconciled from Git.
  • Proven in practice on STACKIT (e.g., published Deloitte platform build): admin cluster keeps app clusters in sync via GitOps; Velero → Object Storage; Alloy agents → central Observability.
  • The hub is your most sensitive cluster — it holds credentials to everything. Minimal tenants: zero.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::06 Multi-Cluster & GitOps
notes.front: KEY DECISION: place the management/GitOps hub on-prem or in STACKIT when the platform must be 'centrally managed from the on-prem DC'?
notes.back:
• Hub on-prem: + control plane physically in your DC (sovereignty optics, direct access to AD/Vault/Git without crossing the VPN); − every reconcile to cloud clusters traverses the VPN; link down = no deploys AND degraded fleet visibility; hub sizing bound to DC capacity.
  • Hub in STACKIT: + adjacent to the fleet (fast, reliable reconciles), survives DC maintenance; on-prem remains authoritative via Git + IdP + Vault (which is what 'centrally managed' really requires); − hub credentials live in cloud; Git unreachable = no new changes (last state keeps reconciling).
  • Middle path: hub in STACKIT, sources of truth (Git, identity, secrets) on-prem, pull-based agents → central management without central fragility.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::06 Multi-Cluster & GitOps
notes.front: Push-based vs. pull-based GitOps for a fleet — compare.
notes.back:
• Push (central Argo CD managing remote clusters): + one pane of glass, instant fleet-wide operations, single install; − hub needs network reachability to EVERY kube-apiserver (through VPN/ACLs), hub stores credentials for all clusters (crown-jewel target), hub outage stalls the fleet.
  • Pull (agent per cluster — Flux, or Argo CD per cluster/agent mode): + outbound-only from clusters (no inbound API exposure), clusters keep reconciling through hub/link outages, scales horizontally; − N installations to upgrade, fleet visibility needs aggregation (dashboards/metrics), bootstrap per cluster.
  • Hybrid architectures bias toward pull, because the WAN link is the least reliable component.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::06 Multi-Cluster & GitOps
notes.front: Argo CD vs. Flux for fleet GitOps — practical differences.
notes.back:
• Argo CD: rich UI + Single Sign-On (SSO) (PingFederate!), AppProject multitenancy, ApplicationSets for fleet generation, sync waves/hooks; heavier footprint; UI can tempt click-ops.
  • Flux: lean controllers, Git/OCI/Helm sources, Kustomize-native, image-update automation, per-cluster by design (pull); no built-in UI (use Weave GitOps/Headlamp/Grafana), multitenancy via Kubernetes RBAC.
  • Both are CNCF-graduated; team familiarity and UI/SSO requirements usually decide. Helm-heavy shops report smoother Helm semantics with Flux's HelmController (real helm upgrade) vs Argo's template-and-diff.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::06 Multi-Cluster & GitOps
notes.front: What do Argo CD ApplicationSets (or Flux equivalents) contribute to multi-cluster operations?
notes.back:
• An ApplicationSet is a template that generates one Application per target from generators: cluster generator (every registered cluster), Git directory/file generator, matrix combinations.
  • Fleet pattern: register/label clusters (env=prod, tier=tenant-a) → ApplicationSets stamp the golden stack and tenant apps onto matching clusters automatically; a new cluster becomes 'just another label match'.
  • Flux equivalent: bootstrap per cluster from a shared repo structure (clusters/<name>/ overlays), optionally templated by Terraform.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::06 Multi-Cluster & GitOps
notes.front: Draw the line: what does Terraform own vs. what does GitOps/Helm own, and why not manage Kubernetes workloads in Terraform?
notes.back:
• Terraform: STACKIT resources — projects, SNA, VPN, SKE clusters + node pools + extensions, managed DBs, DNS, Object Storage, IAM. Plus the one-time in-cluster bootstrap: GitOps agent + its repo credentials.
  • GitOps (Argo/Flux + Helm): everything inside clusters — golden stack, tenant workloads, RBAC, policies.
  • Why not workloads in Terraform: state drift vs. controllers, slow monolithic applies, no continuous reconciliation, plan noise, and the kubeconfig-in-state problem. Terraform hands off; controllers keep truth.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::06 Multi-Cluster & GitOps
notes.front: How do you structure Helm/Kustomize configuration layering so 30 clusters don't become 30 snowflakes?
notes.back:
• One golden-stack repo: base charts/manifests + a values hierarchy: global.yaml → env/prod.yaml → cluster/<name>.yaml (narrowing scope, last wins). Cluster files should be tiny — mostly names/IPs.
  • Choose per component: Helm for parameterized third-party software; Kustomize overlays for your own manifests; umbrella charts sparingly (version-coupling pain).
  • Rules: no manual edits on clusters; every divergence is a values line with a reviewable diff; renovate-bot pins chart versions per ring.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::06 Multi-Cluster & GitOps
notes.front: Walk through the lifecycle: a NEW SKE workload cluster from zero to serving, fully automated.
notes.back:
1. Terraform module instantiated (project/SNA attachment, stackit_ske_cluster, extensions: observability, ACL).
  2. Terraform obtains kubeconfig (stackit_ske_kubeconfig) → installs GitOps agent via Helm provider, registers cluster in the hub (or agent self-registers) with labels (env, tier, tenant).
  3. ApplicationSets match labels → golden stack rolls in (ingress, cert-manager, external-dns, ESO, policies, Alloy, Velero).
  4. ESO pulls secrets (registry creds, Vault access) → tenant apps sync → external-dns publishes records → traffic.
  5. Deletion is the reverse Terraform destroy; state (backups, metrics) survives in Object Storage/central stores.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::06 Multi-Cluster & GitOps
notes.front: Multi-cluster NETWORKING: compare 'independent clusters + DNS' vs. Cilium ClusterMesh vs. Istio multi-cluster vs. Skupper/Submariner.
notes.back:
• Independent + Global Server Load Balancing (GSLB)/DNS: clusters don't know each other; cross-cluster calls go through normal ingress/LB. Simplest, works everywhere, DR-friendly. Default recommendation.
  • Cilium ClusterMesh: pod-to-pod across clusters; needs non-overlapping pod CIDRs, mutual network reachability, and CNI control — risky on managed SKE where you don't own the CNI.
  • Istio multi-cluster (multi-primary or primary-remote + east-west gateways): mutual TLS (mTLS), locality failover, works over LBs without CNI coupling; operationally heavy.
  • Submariner: L3 tunnels between clusters; CNI-adjacent, similar constraints. Skupper: L7 application interconnect, no network coupling — nice for selective hybrid service sharing.
  • Rule: introduce cross-cluster networking only for a named requirement, never 'by default'.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::06 Multi-Cluster & GitOps
notes.front: Disaster Recovery (DR) options when your provider footprint is one STACKIT region with three availability zones + an on-prem DC.
notes.back:
• In-region HA: node pools spread over eu01-1/2/3; zonal-volume awareness for StatefulSets; managed DBs on HA plans.
  • Backup/restore: Velero (manifests + volume snapshots) to Object Storage; DB Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR). Cheapest; hours of Recovery Time Objective (RTO).
  • Pilot light / warm standby: second cluster (other zones or on-prem) with golden stack synced but apps scaled down; restore data on failover.
  • Active-active: both sites serve; needs data-layer replication and GSLB — expensive, only for the few truly critical services.
  • Hybrid bonus: the on-prem DC doubles as the out-of-provider DR site (and vice versa) — a genuine sovereignty argument for hybrid.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::06 Multi-Cluster & GitOps
notes.front: Why is state/data gravity the real constraint of multi-cluster design, and what are the standard answers?
notes.back:
• Stateless workloads move freely between clusters; data does not — block volumes are cluster/zone-local, databases replicate on their own terms.
  • Answers, in order of preference:
    1. Externalize state to managed services (PostgreSQL Flex, Object Storage) reachable from any cluster.
    2. Application-level replication (DB streaming replicas, event sourcing) between sites.
    3. Backup/restore as the fallback consistency story.
  • Anti-pattern: stretching etcd, storage systems, or synchronous replication across the VPN — latency and partition behavior will break you.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::06 Multi-Cluster & GitOps
notes.front: How do you roll out changes across the fleet safely (upgrade rings)?
notes.back:
• Order clusters into rings: lab → dev → staging → prod-canary → prod-rest; promote Git changes (chart versions, K8s minor upgrades) ring by ring with soak time and automated verification (smoke tests, error-budget checks).
  • Stagger SKE maintenance windows to match rings; never let all prod clusters take the same auto-update night.
  • PodDisruptionBudgets + surge-capable node pools keep drains safe; Renovate/CI automates the version bumps so rings are diffs, not manual work.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: Sketch the reference topology: on-prem DC as control center, STACKIT as workload landing zone. What lives where, and what flows over the link?
notes.back:
• On-prem: Active Directory (AD)/Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP), PingFederate, Git + Continuous Integration (CI), Vault/secrets source of truth, Harbor (or registry source), central monitoring/Security Information and Event Management (SIEM), Terraform runners.
  • STACKIT: STACKIT Network Area (SNA) ← VPN/MPLS; projects per team/env; SKE workload clusters (+ optional hub cluster); managed DBs, Object Storage, DNS, Observability.
  • Over the link: GitOps pulls, OIDC/LDAP auth traffic, secret syncs, image replication, telemetry to SIEM, kubectl/Terraform API calls. Not over the link: backups, bulk data, registry pulls at scale (keep those in-region).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: Which IP/CIDR planning rules does a STACKIT hybrid deployment impose?
notes.back:
• STACKIT VPN does no NAT → SNA ranges and on-prem ranges must be non-overlapping; agree the split with the network team BEFORE the first project exists (renumbering later is brutal).
  • Carve the SNA into per-project/per-cluster node-network blocks; document in central IPAM.
  • Pod/Service Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) ranges: may repeat across clusters (they're cluster-internal) — UNLESS you later want ClusterMesh-style pod routing or expose pod IPs on-prem; reserving unique ranges up front keeps that door open.
  • Reserve space for: LB IPs, VPN transfer nets, future DR site, vCluster hosts.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: Design the DNS strategy for on-prem + STACKIT (split-horizon).
notes.back:
• Corporate zones (corp.example.internal): authoritative on on-prem AD DNS.
  • Cloud zones (apps.example.com, cloud.example.internal): STACKIT DNS, records automated by external-dns from cluster ingresses.
  • Cluster → corp names: CoreDNS forwarders (stub domains) pointing to on-prem DNS over the VPN.
  • On-prem → cloud-internal names: conditional forwarders on AD DNS toward the cloud resolver, or publish internal LB records into a corp subzone.
  • Failure mode: VPN down → corp-name resolution in clusters fails; set forwarder timeouts/caching consciously and keep cloud-local dependencies on cloud zones.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: How does central tooling (Terraform, Argo CD, kubectl) on-prem reach the SKE API servers, and how do you secure that path?
notes.back:
• SKE API servers live in STACKIT seeds with public endpoints — reachable from on-prem over the internet by default.
  • Harden: ACL extension allow-listing only your on-prem egress IPs (and VPN ranges where applicable); short-lived credentials via stackit ske kubeconfig login; audit tool identities separately.
  • Design consequence: API access does NOT depend on the VPN (good for break-glass), but data-plane access to internal LBs does.
  • If policy demands no public API exposure at all, verify current SKE private-endpoint options — otherwise that requirement pushes those clusters on-prem.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: Your clusters authenticate users via PingFederate ON-PREM. What does that dependency mean for availability, and how do you mitigate?
notes.back:
• Interactive logins (kubectl OIDC, Argo CD SSO, app SSO) require the on-prem IdP → VPN or internet path to PingFederate becomes an authentication dependency for the whole cloud estate.
  • Mitigations:
    1. Apps validate JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) locally against cached JSON Web Key Sets (JWKS) — existing sessions survive IdP unreachability; only new logins fail.
    2. Reasonable token/refresh lifetimes — balance outage tolerance vs. revocation speed.
    3. Expose PingFederate redundantly (HA pair, dual uplinks) — it is Tier-0 infrastructure.
    4. Break-glass paths that bypass the IdP (sealed admin kubeconfigs, STACKIT-IAM login).
  • Machine traffic (GitOps, ESO) should use non-interactive credentials so deployments don't stop when SSO does.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: Registry strategy for a hybrid fleet when Harbor is your on-prem source of truth — options and failure modes.
notes.back:
• Pull directly from on-prem Harbor: simplest; but every image pull crosses the VPN (capacity!), and link down = pods can't schedule on new nodes. Only acceptable for small fleets.
  • Harbor replication → cloud registry (STACKIT Container Registry or a Harbor in STACKIT): push-based replication rules per project; clusters pull in-region; link outage only delays NEW images. Preferred.
  • Pull-through proxy cache in-region: lazy replication; first pull still crosses the link, cache eviction can bite during incidents.
  • Always: pin digests, pre-pull critical images, keep the golden-stack images replicated with priority; vulnerability-scan at the source (your Trivy/Grype pipeline) and enforce signatures in-cluster.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: Where do CI runners and Terraform executors live — on-prem or in-cloud? Trade-offs.
notes.back:
• On-prem runners: adjacent to Git/Vault/artifacts; reach STACKIT via public APIs (fine); builds pulling cloud data cross the link.
  • In-cluster runners on SKE: adjacent to deploy targets and cloud services; outbound-only access to on-prem Git over VPN; elastic scaling on node pools; but now CI capacity is a cloud tenant to govern (quotas! it's the classic noisy neighbor).
  • Common split: build/test in the cloud near caches and scale; release/state-changing jobs (Terraform apply) from a controlled on-prem runner pool with OIDC federation to STACKIT (no stored keys).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: Compare Terraform state backend options for this platform.
notes.back:
• STACKIT Object Storage (S3 backend): in-cloud, versioned; caveat — classic S3 locking needed DynamoDB, and Terraform ≥1.10 native S3 lockfiles rely on conditional writes: verify support on the S3-compatible endpoint before trusting concurrent applies.
  • PostgreSQL backend on PostgreSQL Flex: real locking out of the box; officially shown in the STACKIT provider docs as a state+locking pattern. Solid cloud-side default.
  • GitLab/Terraform-cloud-style HTTP backend on-prem: state stays in the DC next to CI, access via existing Git auth; adds GitLab as a dependency for all applies.
  • Whatever you pick: state contains secrets (kubeconfigs!) → encrypt, restrict, and never share one state across trust boundaries — split state per project/stack.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: Certificates & PKI: which issuers serve which surface in the hybrid platform?
notes.back:
• Public endpoints: Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME)/Let's Encrypt via cert-manager (DNS-01 against STACKIT DNS for wildcards).
  • Internal services & mutual TLS (mTLS): private Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) — corporate CA (AD CS) or Vault PKI as cert-manager issuer; short-lived certs, automated rotation.
  • Trust distribution: ship the corporate root/intermediates to all clusters (trust-manager) so cloud workloads trust on-prem services and vice versa.
  • Trade-off: AD CS keeps PKI where auditors expect it but is automation-hostile; Vault PKI automates beautifully but adds Vault to the critical path. Many run: offline corp root → Vault as issuing intermediate.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: Centralize observability: how do 10+ SKE clusters feed ONE pane of glass, and where should that pane live?
notes.back:
• Per cluster: a lightweight agent (Grafana Alloy / OpenTelemetry (OTel) Collector) collects metrics, logs, traces and remote-writes outbound — no inbound scraping across the WAN.
  • Backend in STACKIT (Observability service or self-hosted Mimir/Loki/Tempo on a hub cluster): telemetry stays in-region (cheap, link-tolerant); on-prem viewers just need Grafana access. Usually right.
  • Backend on-prem: single sovereign store next to the SIEM; but all telemetry crosses the VPN continuously — budget bandwidth, expect gaps on outage (agents buffer briefly).
  • Compliance middle path: metrics/traces in-region; audit-relevant logs forwarded (filtered!) to the on-prem SIEM via Telemetry Router/Alloy pipelines.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: What is the bandwidth & latency budget discipline for the on-prem↔STACKIT link, given managed VPN tops out at 1 Gbit/s?
notes.back:
• Inventory every flow crossing the link: GitOps pulls (tiny), auth (tiny), secrets sync (tiny), telemetry (can be huge), image replication (bursty, large), backups (must NOT cross), user traffic to internal LBs (depends).
  • Keep heavy flows in-region: Velero→Object Storage, registry pulls from in-region replica, logs aggregated in-region with filtered forwarding.
  • Latency: AuthN round-trips and synchronous cross-site calls are the killers — design services to be site-local with async replication.
  • If the honest budget exceeds ~1 Gbit/s sustained or needs latency guarantees → MPLS/dedicated connectivity, VPN as failover (BGP).

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: Egress control: should cloud workloads reach the internet directly, or hairpin through on-prem inspection? Trade-offs.
notes.back:
• Hairpin all egress via VPN → on-prem proxy/firewall: single inspection/policy point (SIEM-friendly, familiar to security), but consumes scarce VPN bandwidth, adds latency, and the proxy becomes a fleet-wide SPOF.
  • Cloud-local egress with policy: NetworkPolicy egress rules + DNS-based filtering + security groups; scalable and link-independent, but policy now lives in two stacks and L7 inspection needs an in-cloud proxy.
  • Pragmatic: cloud-local egress for platform traffic (registries, APIs) with tight allow-lists; hairpin only flows your compliance framework explicitly requires to be inspected.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: Backup & restore architecture for the whole platform (clusters + data), hybrid edition.
notes.back:
• Cluster state: Velero per cluster → in-region Object Storage (manifests + CSI volume snapshots); schedule daily volumes / weekly full-cluster; test restores into a scratch cluster regularly — untested backups are hopes, not backups.
  • Managed DBs: built-in automated backups + PITR; export logical dumps to Object Storage for provider-independent copies.
  • Cross-site copies: replicate the backup buckets (or dump exports) to on-prem storage for sovereignty/DR-from-provider-loss — this is a scheduled bulk job; run it off-peak and NOT through the same VPN plan that carries production auth traffic if volumes are large.
  • Git is a backup too: the entire desired state must be reconstructible from Git + secrets store + backups. Rebuild-from-scratch time IS your real RTO.

notes.deck: STACKIT Hybrid Cloud Architect::07 Hybrid & Central Management
notes.front: Final synthesis: name the seven pillars that make 'centrally managed from on-prem' actually work on STACKIT.
notes.back:
1. Landing zone: org/folders/projects via Terraform modules; SNA with clean IPAM.
  2. Connectivity: managed VPN (BGP, active-active) or MPLS into the SNA; non-overlapping CIDRs.
  3. Identity: AD → PingFederate (OIDC) → clusters (Pinniped or native) + Argo SSO; STACKIT service accounts with OIDC federation for machines.
  4. Delivery: Git on-prem as single source of truth; pull-based GitOps agents; Terraform for infra only.
  5. Distribution: registry replication in-region; secrets via central store + ESO.
  6. Operations: fleet observability with in-region storage + SIEM forwarding; Velero + DB backups; upgrade rings.
  7. Governance: tenancy model per trust/compliance zone; quotas at every layer; policy engine + image signing enforced fleet-wide.
